t: Handle pharmacy refill calls with a voice agent
s: A pharmacy's phone agent identifies callers, submits refills, and routes renewal requests to prescribers.
did: The pharmacy put a voice agent on its refill line. It confirms who is calling, checks the prescription, submits the refill, or queues a renewal request for the prescriber.
how: It handled about 380 refills in its first 30 days. Calls it can't resolve go to staff.
pre: A pharmacy system the agent can query
A phone line you can route
A vendor agreement that covers patient data
limits: Identifying a caller by voice is the weak point: accents, background noise and bad lines all raise the chance of matching the wrong patient record.
380 refills is self-reported with no error rate beside it, so there is no way to tell how many were wrong.
No approval step is described, so a misheard drug or dose reaches the prescriber queue unchecked.
ideas: Require a second identifier, such as date of birth, before any refill is submitted.
Log every call where the match was low-confidence and review those weekly rather than sampling at random.

t: Book property viewings and follow up with leads
s: An n8n sales assistant books site visits, sends follow-up emails, and updates the CRM for a real-estate team.
did: The builder connected n8n to email, a calendar and the CRM. The agent answers lead questions, offers viewing times, books them, and logs each step.
how: It runs daily with no manual booking. The poster didn't share conversion numbers.
pre: An n8n instance, cloud or self-hosted
A mailbox the agent can send from
limits: No conversion figures were shared, so there is no evidence booked viewings became deals.
It emails leads with no approval step, so a misread question goes out in the agency's name.
Double-booking is the usual failure here, when two leads are offered the same slot at once.
ideas: Hold slots provisionally and confirm only once the lead replies.
Compare no-show rates against manually booked viewings to see whether speed costs quality.

t: Reconcile supplier invoices and invoice clients automatically
s: A business owner's agent matches supplier invoices, reports pricing and freight, and invoices clients through Zoho Books.
did: The owner built a small CRM with an agent behind it. It reads supplier invoices, matches them to orders, places supplier orders, and raises client invoices through the Zoho Books API.
how: Reconciliation that took hours now runs on its own, with a pricing and freight report as a bonus.
pre: Supplier invoices in a predictable format
limits: It places supplier orders and raises client invoices with no approval step, so a matching error becomes a real financial transaction.
Invoice matching is brittle when suppliers change their layouts, which they do without warning.
"Hours now runs on its own" says nothing about how often the matches are wrong.
ideas: Hold any order above a value threshold for a person to release.
Reconcile against the bank feed monthly to catch silent mismatches.

t: Triage dealership customer texts by sentiment
s: A car dealership group's Make flow reads customer texts, closes routine ones, and flags unhappy customers.
did: Every inbound text runs through a sentiment check. Routine messages get closed with a reply; negative ones go straight to the aftersales team.
how: It auto-closed about 18,000 of 47,000 messages, so staff only saw the ones that needed a person.
pre: An SMS platform with an API
An agreed definition of what counts as negative
limits: Sentiment is a crude proxy for urgency: a calmly worded message about a safety fault reads as routine.
18,000 of 47,000 auto-closed is a volume figure, not evidence that none of those customers needed a person.
Short replies and sarcasm are exactly where sentiment scoring is least reliable.
ideas: Sample closed conversations weekly and measure how many should have been escalated.
Route on safety and legal keywords regardless of what the sentiment score says.

t: Screen job candidates and handle outreach
s: A Make scenario parses resumes, scores candidates, updates the ATS, and sends shortlists to recruiters in Slack.
did: Resumes land in a folder. The flow extracts each one, scores it against the role, writes the result to the ATS, emails an acknowledgment, and posts a shortlist to Slack.
how: Published as a vendor how-to, so no real-world results are reported.
limits: Automated resume scoring carries real discrimination risk, and in several jurisdictions it is regulated.
This was published as a vendor how-to with no real results, so the scoring quality is untested.
Scoring against a job description rewards people who write resumes well, which is not the same as doing the job well.
ideas: Keep every score with the reasoning behind it, so a rejected candidate's file can be audited.
Run it alongside human screening for a month and compare who each would have advanced.

t: Mark student reports and build an assessment dashboard
s: A primary teacher had Claude build an app that marks reports, plus a dashboard for assessment data.
did: The teacher described the marking rubric and the data they track. Claude built a marking app, a dashboard, and a skill that lines up lesson ideas with the curriculum.
how: Marking time dropped, and the dashboard replaced a manual spreadsheet.
limits: Consistency across a large batch is the open question: the same work can score differently in different sessions.
Student work is sensitive, and school policy may not allow putting it into a third-party tool at all.
Time saved is reported; agreement with the teacher's own marks is not.
ideas: Re-mark a sample blind and measure how far the scores drift.
Ask for the rubric line behind every mark, so a disagreement can be traced.

t: Split scanned homework and log it per student
s: A Claude Code skill reads names on batch scans, splits the PDF per student, and updates the completion sheet.
did: Teachers scan a stack of handwritten homework in one go. The skill reads each name, matches it to the class roster, splits the PDF, and marks the tracker.
how: Missing work gets flagged automatically, which used to take a manual pass every week.
pre: A scanner that outputs one PDF
limits: Reading handwritten names is the failure point, and similar names in one class make it worse.
A misfiled page is logged as another student's work, which is easy to miss and awkward to unpick.
There is no approval step, so mistakes reach the tracker directly.
ideas: Flag low-confidence name matches for a quick visual check instead of filing them.
Reconcile the tracker against the scanned page count to catch anything dropped.

t: Redline a contract as Word tracked changes
s: A lawyer had Claude rewrite two sections of a 30-page document and reply to comments as tracked changes.
did: Working inside Word, the lawyer asked Claude to revise two sections and answer the reviewer comments, keeping every edit as a native tracked change.
how: The lawyer judged the result better than Microsoft's built-in assistant and kept full control of what to accept.
pre: The contract and the reviewer comments
limits: One lawyer's judgement on two sections is not evidence that it holds across contract types.
A redline shows the changes made; the change that should have been made and was not is invisible.
Interactions between clauses across a long agreement are where this is weakest.
ideas: Ask separately what it chose not to change, and why.
Check the output against the firm's precedent clauses rather than judging the edit on its own.

t: Cut a hospital bill using Medicare price analysis
s: Claude priced every billing code on a $195,628 hospital bill against Medicare rates; the patient then negotiated.
did: The patient shared the itemized bill. Claude built a spreadsheet of Medicare prices for each code, showing where charges ran far above them.
how: Using that analysis, the patient negotiated about $163,000 off. The patient wrote the letters; Claude only analyzed.
pre: The itemised bill, with billing codes
limits: The $163,000 came from one negotiation: the analysis created leverage, but the outcome was the hospital's decision.
Medicare rates are a benchmark, not a price a private payer is obliged to accept.
A misread billing code sends the whole comparison off, and codes are easy to transcribe wrong.
ideas: Spot-check a sample of codes against the published fee schedule before relying on the table.
Ask which charges are most often reduced in negotiation, not only where the gap is largest.

t: Calculate US taxes from 1099s and brokerage statements
s: ChatGPT computed a full US tax picture from 1099s, a self-employment spreadsheet, and brokerage statements.
did: The poster uploaded their 1099 forms, a spreadsheet of self-employed income and expenses, and brokerage statements, then asked for the full calculation.
how: The numbers matched a professional's result in their case study.
limits: Matching a professional once, on one return, is not evidence that it generalises to other situations.
Cost basis and wash sales on brokerage statements are where this most often goes wrong.
You remain liable for the filing regardless of what produced the numbers.
ideas: Have it show the calculation line by line so each figure can be checked against the form.
Run last year's return, where the answer is already known, as a test.

t: Run Meta ad campaigns for a newsletter
s: A Claude Code agent made ad images, ran Meta campaigns through the API, and built landing-page variants.
did: The agent generated creative, launched and adjusted campaigns via the Meta API, built landing page variants, and pulled analytics each day.
how: About 50 variants were tested over 31 days. The write-up shares the process more than the final cost per subscriber.
pre: A spend cap you are willing to lose
limits: It spends real money and posts publicly with no approval step, which is the riskiest combination on this site.
Cost per subscriber is not reported, so there is no way to know whether 50 variants beat one good ad.
Automated creative can breach ad policy, and that risks the whole account rather than one campaign.
ideas: Set the hard spend cap at the ad account level, not inside the agent.
Hold creative for review before it goes live; the cost is a short delay.

t: Find technical SEO problems and generate the fixes
s: An SEO agent crawled a site, found broken canonicals and orphaned pages, ranked them, and wrote code fixes.
did: The author tested five SEO agents. The best one browsed the whole site, listed issues by likely impact, and produced the code changes for each.
how: It found broken canonical tags, orphaned pages, and missing schema; two other agents only pulled Search Console data.
pre: A site the agent can crawl
Access to make the code changes
limits: The issues it found are easy to verify; the issues it missed are invisible.
Ranking by likely impact is a guess at how search engines weight things, not a measurement.
Generated fixes still need testing: a wrong canonical tag does more damage than a missing one.
ideas: Run it against a site whose problems you already know, to measure what it misses.
Apply fixes in small batches so any ranking change can be attributed.

t: Reorder low stock from suppliers automatically
s: Each morning a system checks Shopify inventory and emails a ready-made order to the right supplier.
did: The store owner set reorder levels per product. A daily job compares stock against them and emails the matching supplier a pre-written order.
how: Stockouts stopped, and the owner no longer checks inventory by hand.
pre: Stock levels in a system that can be queried
limits: It emails real orders with no approval step, so a bad stock count becomes a real purchase.
Fixed thresholds do not understand seasonality, so it over-orders after an unusual week.
"Stockouts stopped" says nothing about whether stock on hand rose and tied up cash.
ideas: Hold orders above a value for release and let the rest go.
Track stock turn alongside stockouts, so the fix is not simply more inventory.

t: Answer support tickets from Freshdesk history
s: A SaaS owner connected ChatGPT to Freshdesk and internal tools, then pulled back from full autonomy.
did: The agent could read past tickets and use internal tools to draft and send answers.
how: Picking the right answer, and knowing when not to answer, proved unreliable. It now drafts and a person sends.
pre: A body of past tickets to learn from
limits: The reported failure was knowing when not to answer, which is the hard part of support automation.
Past tickets teach it what was said before, including the answers that were wrong.
Draft-and-review saves less than it looks once a person reads every draft.
ideas: Let it answer only the ticket types where it scored well, and stay silent on the rest.
Measure how much drafts are edited before sending, to see where it actually helps.

t: Handle store customer support with an AI agent
s: A merchant ran Gorgias's AI agent for months, then switched it off.
did: The agent answered customer emails and chats for an online store.
how: It gave irrelevant answers and promised things the store couldn't deliver, so the merchant disabled it.
pre: Policy documents that are actually accurate
limits: Promising what the store could not deliver is worse than no answer: it creates obligations.
Failures like this usually trace to missing grounding rather than a weak model.
Sending to customers with no approval step means mistakes land before anyone sees them.
ideas: Ground every answer in the policy documents and refuse anything they do not cover.
Start in draft mode and enable sending only for question types with a clean record.

t: Run a contractor's back-office paperwork
s: A contractor's agent flagged an insurance certificate mismatch, created work orders, and filled a credit application.
did: The agent read contracts and certificates in the contractor's files and email, then produced work orders and forms.
how: It caught an insurance discrepancy before a job started, which the contractor said would have been missed.
pre: Contracts and certificates in one searchable place
limits: One caught discrepancy is a good anecdote, not a detection rate.
What it misses stays silent, and an insurance gap only surfaces at claim time.
It reads a whole mailbox and file store, which is broad access for a back-office task.
ideas: Run it over closed jobs where the problems are already known, to see what it misses.
Have it report expiring certificates on a schedule rather than only when asked.

t: Turn orders into Xero purchase orders, invoices and bills
s: A Make setup creates Xero purchase orders from monday.com, emails client invoices, and matches supplier bills.
did: When an order changes status in monday.com, the flow creates the Xero PO, sends the client invoice, and matches uploaded supplier invoices to bills.
how: Anything that fails to match is flagged for a person instead of guessed.
limits: It sends client invoices with no approval step, so a status changed at the wrong moment bills a client early.
Flagging what fails to match is good, but a confident wrong match is never flagged.
Accounting errors compound quietly and surface at period close.
ideas: Hold the first invoice to each new client for a person to release.
Reconcile created documents against monday statuses weekly to catch false matches.

t: Automate a bookkeeping firm's routine workflows
s: A bookkeeping firm used n8n to automate recurring client work.
did: Repetitive steps such as collecting statements, chasing documents and preparing entries became n8n workflows.
how: The firm estimates about 600 hours saved a year.
limits: 600 hours a year is the firm's own estimate, with no method shown.
Chasing documents automates well; the judgement in preparing entries does not.
Holding many clients' credentials in one automation concentrates the damage from any breach.
ideas: Measure rework time too, since hours saved upstream can reappear as corrections.
Keep credentials separated per client so one failure does not expose the rest.

t: Turn bug reports into fix pull requests
s: Sentry's analysis hands the root cause to a Cursor cloud agent, which writes the fix and opens a PR.
did: When Sentry finds the root cause of an error, it passes the context to Cursor's agent. The agent writes a fix and opens a pull request in the repo.
how: Developers review and merge the PR, so nothing ships without a person.
pre: A repo the agent can open PRs against
limits: A fix that stops the error is not always the right fix; it can mask the cause instead.
Review quality drops when plausible-looking PRs arrive steadily.
It only sees errors Sentry caught, so silent failures stay untouched.
ideas: Require a failing test in the PR that the fix makes pass.
Track how many of these PRs are later reverted.

t: Move a company website off its CMS
s: Cursor agents moved a company site from a CMS to code and Markdown in three days.
did: The engineer had agents convert content and refactor the site, with sub-agents splitting the broad changes.
how: It took three days and about $260 in model costs.
pre: The repo and a CMS export
limits: Three days and about $260 describes one migration; cost scales with site size and how messy the content is.
Content conversion loses things quietly, and embeds, redirects and metadata are the usual casualties.
Splitting broad changes across sub-agents makes review harder, because nobody saw the whole diff.
ideas: Diff the rendered pages before and after, rather than reviewing the code changes.
Check that every old URL still resolves; migrations are where link equity is lost.

t: Watch for and book a hard-to-get restaurant table
s: A travel agent watched a popular restaurant for an opening, booked a table for two, and texted confirmation.
did: The user named the restaurant and party size. The agent checked for openings until one appeared, then booked it.
how: It secured an 8:45pm table and sent a text confirmation.
pre: An account on the restaurant's booking platform
limits: Polling a booking site repeatedly can get the account rate-limited or banned.
It books with no approval step, so you are committed to whatever slot it finds.
Many booking platforms treat automation as a terms violation.
ideas: Have it alert you when a slot opens instead of confirming outright.
Set the acceptable time window narrowly so it cannot book something you will not use.

t: Screen new founders for venture investing
s: An investor's agents watch new company filings, research founders, and draft outreach to promising matches.
did: The system monitors new filings, researches each founder, flags ones that match the fund's thesis, then drafts outreach and preps meeting questions.
how: Outreach and scheduling run without the investor doing first-pass research.
limits: It drafts and sends outreach with no approval step, and a bad first email burns the relationship.
Screening against a thesis reinforces it: the fund stops seeing what sits outside the pattern.
Researching founders pulls personal information, which brings data protection obligations.
ideas: Keep a log of the founders it screened out and review it quarterly for misses.
Hold the first message for a person while the hit rate is still unproven.

t: Handle product questions, warranties and returns by voice
s: A consumer electronics brand rebuilt its global phone support on voice agents in several languages.
did: Voice agents answer product questions, process warranty claims and start returns, in multiple languages.
how: Reported in a vendor case study; figures are the vendor's own.
pre: Order and warranty systems with APIs
A decision on which languages to cover
limits: The figures come from a vendor case study and are the vendor's own, with no independent check.
Starting returns and warranty claims commits the company to money without an approval step.
Multilingual quality is rarely even, and the weakest language is usually the least measured.
ideas: Publish containment and escalation rates per language rather than one blended number.
Cap the value of a return the agent can start on its own.

t: Handle follow-ups after every meeting
s: An agent finds the transcript, pulls out action items, messages teammates, and books the next meeting.
did: After a meeting ends, the agent reads the transcript, lists action items, posts them to Slack, and checks calendars to schedule a follow-up.
how: Shown as a vendor demo, so no real-world results are reported.
limits: This is a vendor demo with no real results, so the accuracy of the action items is unknown.
Transcripts miss what was agreed with a nod, and tend to invent structure that was not there.
It posts to Slack and schedules with no approval, so a wrong action item becomes a commitment.
ideas: Post the action items to the organiser as a draft first.
Measure how many items get edited or deleted after posting.

t: Coordinate a family member's medical records and care
s: A family gave a relative's records to an agent, which caught a medication schedule error and a transcription mistake.
did: The family used the agent as a coordinator across doctors, records and test results.
how: It flagged a wrong pain-medication schedule and an error in genetic test markers, which changed the treatment plan.
pre: Records and test results gathered in one place
Agreement from the family on what it may read
limits: Catching two errors is a strong anecdote, but the misses are invisible and the stakes here are clinical.
A confident wrong reading of a medication schedule is more dangerous than any other failure on this site.
It holds a complete medical history in one place, which is a serious concentration of sensitive data.
ideas: Treat every flag as a question for the care team, never as an instruction.
Have it cite the document and line behind each flag so a clinician can check it quickly.

t: Collect grant listings from many countries
s: A Zapier agent searches the web for grants in different countries and adds them to Airtable.
did: The agent runs searches by country and program type, then writes each grant it finds as a row in Airtable.
how: It works, but the user is still tuning which results to keep.
pre: A list of countries and programme types
limits: It is still being tuned for which results to keep, which is the actual work.
Search-based collection misses grants that are poorly indexed, and those are often the least contested.
Closed and expired listings get collected alongside open ones unless dates are checked.
ideas: Record where each grant was found, so sources that never yield can be dropped.
Check the deadline on write and discard anything already closed.

t: Draft an evidence-backed insurance appeal
s: ChatGPT helped build an employment insurance appeal that was accepted, and a home flooding appeal.
did: The user gave ChatGPT the denial letter, policy terms and evidence, then built the appeal argument point by point.
how: The employment insurance appeal was accepted.
limits: One accepted appeal, in one jurisdiction, under one policy.
An argument can read as well-structured while resting on a misread clause.
Deadlines and required forms vary, and a strong argument filed late fails anyway.
ideas: Ask it to quote the exact policy wording behind each argument, so the reading can be checked.
Have it name the weakest point and what evidence would strengthen it before you file.

t: Find and parse chemical safety data sheets
s: An app built with Manus finds the right SDS PDF online, downloads it, and turns it into structured data.
did: Given a product name, the system searches for the safety data sheet, downloads the PDF, extracts the text and maps it to a fixed schema.
how: The author built almost the whole app through Manus.
pre: The product names to look up
Somewhere to store the PDFs and parsed output
limits: The right-looking sheet may be the wrong revision, and safety data changes between versions.
PDF extraction is uneven, and the sections that matter most are often the worst formatted.
There is no approval step on data people may rely on when handling chemicals.
ideas: Capture the revision date and source URL with every sheet, and re-check on a schedule.
Validate the parsed schema against a set of known-good sheets before trusting it.
